## Course description

The course will guide students through the design, execution, and communication of an economics research project. It emphasizes research judgment, reproducible workflows, responsible use of AI, writing clarity, and the ability to explain one's work.

## Learning objectives

By the end of the semester, students will be able to:

| Course competency | Broader purpose |
|:---|:---|
| Formulate an original research question | Develop creativity and taste |
| Organize a version-controlled, one-click reproducible research pipeline | Practice structured automation |
| Use AI productively for research and coding | Treat AI as a complement rather than a substitute |
| Write a clear research paper | Use writing to clarify, test, and develop ideas |
| Communicate progress concisely in writing and in meetings | Learn to "manage up" effectively |
| Provide constructive feedback on peer projects | Build collaboration-based social skills |
| Present and defend the project's research design, analysis, code, and conclusions | Strengthen verbal communication |

: {tbl-colwidths="[60,40]"}

## Course format

- 8 class meetings will be lectures. Each lecture will have a small but mandatory assignment to complete beforehand. The goal is to have the lectures be interactive, so thoughtfully engaging with the assigned material and completing the mandatory assignment prior to class is essential.

- 12 class meetings will be research meetings. Students will rotate between scheduled 1-on-1 meetings with the instructor or TA. At least 24 hours before each 1-on-1 meeting, the student will submit a meeting-specific GitHub issue (see [bottom of syllabus](#individual-meeting-preparation) for details). When the student is not in a 1-on-1 meeting, they will be in assigned small groups to do a project-related exercise or provide structured peer feedback.

- 2 class meetings will focus exclusively on small-group writing exercises.

- 4 class meetings will be presentations in front of your peers.

- The final exam will be a closed-book, individualized written exam assessing the student's understanding of their code and project.

## Grading

Final grade calculation:

- 15% pre-class assignments and meeting-preparation issues
- 5% paper outline (due Monday October 19 by 10:30am)
- 5% initial paper draft (due Monday November 2 by 10:30am)
- 10% revised paper draft (due Wednesday November 18 by 10:30am)
- 20% final paper (due Friday December 4 by 11:59pm)
- 5% final code quality and reproducibility (due Friday December 4 by 11:59pm)
- 15% final presentation (December 7 or December 9)
- 25% final exam (final exam period)

## Attendance

In-person attendance is mandatory. Feedback with the professor, the TA, and peers is a core component of the class. There will be a full final letter grade deduction for more than two unexcused absences. The Wednesday class before Thanksgiving will meet but will not count as an unexcused absence if missed.

## Laptop and cell phone use

No cell phone use is allowed during any class meeting for any reason, while laptops are permitted for only limited use. Laptops are permitted for individual meetings with the instructor or TA for reviewing the GitHub issue at hand but not allowed during lectures. During peer feedback group meetings, the student sharing results or soliciting feedback is allowed to use a laptop but the others are not. The rationale is that randomized controlled trials at universities demonstrate the learning benefits of prohibiting [laptop](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0272775716303454) and [cell phone](https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=5370727) use.

## Artificial intelligence use

AI is a part of the modern research process and thus within the course's subject matter. The course's structure and AI policy are intended to encourage student behavior that facilitates learning. Students are expected to use tools in ways that support their reasoning abilities rather than replace them. Students must understand and be accountable for all of their work. 

Because the iterative process of revising writing is a necessary foundational skill, AI usage is explicitly forbidden for one component of the class: writing prose in papers. All prose--the written text that appears as words in paper drafts--must be manually drafted and edited by students. Therefore, students must manually use Google Docs while connected to the internet when drafting prose.

Students are expected to comply with this policy in the spirit of mutual respect, but the instructor and TA will ensure compliance using several verification steps. Specifically, the instructor and TA will audit the edit history to ensure it was done manually and reserve the right to use AI writing detection software. Any suspected violations will be reported to MIT's Office of Student Conduct and Community Standards.

## Required text and materials

- Varanya Chaubey, *[The Little Book of Research Writing](https://www.amazon.com/Little-Book-Research-Writing/dp/1974673162)*.
- Three months of a $20-per-month subscription to an approved frontier LLM (e.g., Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini) for use with exclusively low-risk, non-Institute data. If you are using at least medium-risk Institute data, then you must use an MIT [Parley account](https://orgchart.mit.edu/letters/parley-api-now-available-mit-community-undergraduate-students). Note that Parley does not include frontier models, relies on variable usage pricing, and provides undergraduates with only $10 of monthly API credits. Refer to [MIT's Generative AI usage policy guidance](https://ist.mit.edu/ai) for more detail.

## Accessibility and accommodations

MIT is committed to the principle of equal access. Students who need disability accommodations are encouraged to speak with Disability and Access Services (DAS), prior to or early in the semester so that accommodation requests can be evaluated and addressed in a timely fashion.

The instructor and TA are ready to assist with any approved accommodations. Please inform the TA, who will oversee accommodation implementation for this course.

## Late submissions

The course structure scaffolds assignments to build on one another, so it is highly encouraged to submit all assignments on time. Late submission grades are penalized 25 points (out of 100 total potential points) per delayed day to incentivize timely submissions. The only exception is for a documented accommodation from MIT's Student Support Services (S3).

## Inclusion

Course participants will refer to one another using each person's preferred first name. Using preferred first names rather than pronouns has two purposes: engender a collegial atmosphere and avoid unintentional misgendering. Students will be provided name cards to facilitate learning each other's names. The one exception is for communicating with the instructor: please address the instructor and all other faculty members as 'Professor [Last Name]' in speech and email, unless expressly invited to do otherwise. The purpose is to maintain professional equity and respect for all instructors.

Students are expected to be respectful when providing peer feedback. A growth mindset is useful when receiving feedback, but this is difficult to do when the feedback is ad hominem or destructive rather than substantive and constructive. Students should report any concerns to either the instructor or TA.

## Course Feedback

The course is structured to facilitate learning, but the instructor and TA are open to your feedback on how it can be improved. There will be a formal process at the course midpoint for collecting and addressing feedback on what's going well and what's not going well. But students are encouraged to anonymously send in constructive feedback to [this form](https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSfiJ3Ash9kRQoSbOJtbyCOc8oxiTNxpTRo4AWuMAIoezVq9kA/viewform?usp=sharing&ouid=107655664528523787088) at any point in the semester.

## Individual meeting preparation {#individual-meeting-preparation}

This section details how students will prepare agendas for their 1-on-1 meetings. At least 24 hours before the meeting, the student will open a meeting-specific issue in their GitHub repository using the template below. The instructor or TA will prepare for the meeting by reading the meeting agenda issue beforehand. The suggested word count for the agenda is approximately 250 words, excluding links and tables. Students should focus on results and decisions rather than time spent (e.g., write “Estimated the baseline specification and found...” rather than “Worked on regressions”).

Students will use the following labels for both the overall project and the next course deliverable:

- **On track:** Progress can continue without intervention.
- **At risk:** A problem could affect the project or deliverable, but there is a plausible path forward.
- **Blocked:** Progress requires a decision or assistance that is not independently obtainable.

Students are required to link to evidence in their GitHub repository within the meeting agenda. They are highly encouraged to use separate GitHub issues for tracking consequential unresolved decisions or incomplete tasks. When collecting evidence on major decisions, they are also highly encouraged to test alternatives on short-lived branches.

For concreteness, suppose an unresolved decision is about the main sample composition. The student would create a separate issue titled "Choose the appropriate sample definition," which would be automatically numbered by GitHub (e.g., #23). The student could test alternatives on branches named `23-full-sample` and `23-restricted-sample` and summarize the key differences in a comparison table in issue #23. The meeting agenda would link to issue #23 as an unresolved decision. Once a decision is made, the student would record the rationale in issue #23, merge the chosen branch into the main branch, and close issue #23.

After the meeting, students will update the agenda with next steps and record any resolved decisions in the linked decision issues.

### 1-on-1 meeting agenda issue template

Title the issue `Meeting preparation — YYYY-MM-DD`.

#### 1. Bottom line

- **Overall project:** On track / At risk / Blocked (one-sentence explanation)
- **Next course deliverable:** Name and due date
- **Deliverable status:** On track / At risk / Blocked (one-sentence explanation)
- **Goal for this meeting:** By the end of the meeting, I want to have decided or resolved...

#### 2. Current project state

**Work modes:** Not started / Building / Testing / Revising / Rebuilding / Holding steady

For each row, select the progress description that best represents what is currently usable and the work mode that best represents your current focus.

**2a. Research components**

| Component | Current progress | Primary work mode |
|---|---|---|
| Research question | None / Candidate questions / Working question | Select one work mode |
| Data | None / Candidate sources / Raw data / Analysis dataset / Documented quality checks | Select one work mode |
| Analysis | None / Analysis ideas / Documented descriptives / Baseline estimate / Reproducible baseline | Select one work mode |

: {tbl-colwidths="[25,45,30]"}

**2b. Paper writing**

**Writing artifacts:** None / Notes or outline / Partial draft / Complete working draft

| Paper section | Current usable artifact | Primary work mode |
|---|---|---|
| Data | Select one writing artifact | Select one work mode |
| Methodology | Select one writing artifact | Select one work mode |
| Results | Select one writing artifact | Select one work mode |
| Introduction | Select one writing artifact | Select one work mode |

#### 3. Progress and learnings

Report concrete findings rather than activities or time spent. Findings can be unexpected results or newly-discovered roadblocks.

- **Finding:** Brief description + link to evidence
- **Finding:** Brief description + link to evidence

**Implication:** How did this help you make progress on the project? How does it inform the project's next steps?

#### 4. Decisions, questions, or blockers

Include 1-3 items, ordered by descending importance. For a blocker, include what you have already tried and the specific help needed in the brief description.

1. **Decision, question, or blocker:** Brief description
   - **Context and evidence:** Link to a separate issue, or provide 1–2 sentences explaining the relevant context and evidence.
   - **Preliminary recommendation and reasoning (pre-meeting):** Completed prior to the meeting with the perceived best path forward
   - **Next steps (post-meeting):** Completed after the meeting before resolving the meeting agenda, potentially linking to newly-created GitHub issues
2. ...
3. ...

#### 5. Committed next steps

Draft this section prior to the meeting and revise this section after the meeting. List 1-3 commitments. Each commitment should identify an observable output, its target date, and what will count as complete.

1. **Specific deliverable (target date):** One-sentence completion criterion + optional link to GitHub issue
2. ...
3. ...
